messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Elias was twenty-one, a social ministry worker newly married, when he volunteered for a three-month relief deployment in a conflict zone. His team was stationed near a village that had been shelled, distributing food and medical supplies. One afternoon, a truck backfired near the checkpoint. Elias heard shouting in Arabic—angry, urgent—and then the crack of gunfire. He dove behind a wall, his heart slamming, and for what felt like hours he lay there, certain he would die, the voices growing louder and closer before suddenly stopping. When he finally stood, the village was quiet, the shouting had ceased, and the danger was over. But the memory of that terror did not fade; it lodged itself inside him, and months later, back home in his quiet American town, the sound of a raised voice in a grocery store could send him right back behind that wall.

Now, Elias cannot bear to talk about what happened. When his wife asks about his deployment, or when a coworker mentions a military family in need, the memory surges forward—not as a story he tells, but as a vivid, present terror that feels as real as the moment it happened. The memory is so extreme, so far outside anything he had ever known, that sometimes he wonders if it really happened to him at all. Yet the terror is undeniable: remembering brings back the same helplessness, the same certainty of death, and the memory feels like it is happening right now, not something that is over. These episodes leave him shaken, and he has come to believe that if he talks about the event, he will be pulled back into that moment and never fully return.

To cope, Elias has developed a careful set of routines. He avoids any situation that might make him feel happy or hopeful, because hope feels like a trap—a vulnerability that could be shattered. He stays up until very late at night, delaying sleep, because the moment he closes his eyes the memory is waiting for him, and he would rather be exhausted than relive it. When he does sleep, he wakes during the night to check that he is safe—listening for footsteps, for the wrong kind of silence. This hypervigilance has bled into his days: sudden movements by others put him immediately on guard, and strangers approaching him in ordinary situations feel like threats. He has come to believe that the world is filled with hidden dangers, and that he must stay watchful to survive.

The more Elias ruminate on how the event could have been prevented—if he had been faster, if he had stayed behind the wall sooner—the more the memory intrudes, sharp and terrifying, and the more threatened he feels by the ordinary world around him. Every raised voice in Arabic he hears on the street or in a store triggers the same terror, and each trigger strengthens his belief that the memory is not really over, that it could happen again at any moment. His wife has noticed he no longer joins her for dinner with friends; he says he is tired, but what he cannot tell her is that he is afraid of letting his guard down, afraid that a moment of happiness will leave him defenseless.

He came to therapy because his marriage is fraying and his work is suffering. What frightens him most is the thought that this will never end—that he will always be a man hiding behind a wall, listening for the shouting to start again.

violation_explanations: No paragraph explicitly states that triggers (e.g., raised voices) cause or lead to maladaptive strategies (e.g., avoidance, hypervigilance); they are described as co-occurring or as separate consequences.
No paragraph explicitly states that triggers cause or lead to a sense of threat; the text describes them as eliciting terror and intrusions but not directly causing a feeling of danger.
No paragraph explicitly states that triggers cause or lead to the trauma memory; triggers are described as bringing back terror or sending him behind the wall, but not as causing the memory itself.

No paragraph explicitly states that the memory causes or leads to maladaptive strategies; the memory is described as something he avoids and that waits for him, but not as the direct cause of his routines.
No paragraph explicitly states that the memory causes or leads to a sense of threat; the memory brings terror and helplessness, but not a direct feeling of danger.
No paragraph explicitly states that the memory causes or leads to triggers; the memory is described as being triggered by sounds, but not as causing those triggers.
No paragraph explicitly states that a sense of threat causes or leads to the memory; threat is described as a consequence of triggers and hypervigilance, not as causing the memory.
No paragraph explicitly states that a sense of threat causes or leads to triggers; threat is described as a state that leads to hypervigilance but not as causing triggers.
No paragraph explicitly states that maladaptive strategies cause or lead to the memory; the strategies are described as coping mechanisms that prevent or delay the memory, not as causing it.
